moves.sectionTitle: Positions, semantics, and the scope of realism
moves.speaker: Eric Sampson
moves.proposition: Moral realism combines cognitivism, non-nihilism, and the stance-independent truth of at least some moral beliefs.

sourceSpan.excerpt: So one is cognitivism. It's the view that when we make judgments, at least some of them are attempting to describe the world as it is, their expressions of beliefs, the non-nihilism. So at least some of those beliefs are true. And when they're true, they're true stance independently, that is independent of anybody's opinions or reactions. They don't depend on a culture's reactions. They don't depend on mine. They don't depend on what I like.

moves.argumentDescription: Sampson defines realism as cognitivism, non-nihilism, and the stance-independent truth of at least some moral beliefs, thereby fixing a deliberately limited affirmative target.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The three-part definition cleanly separates truth-evaluable moral belief, the existence of some moral truths, and independence from individual or cultural reactions, establishing an unusually precise motion-level target. Principal limitation: Definition supplies conceptual organization rather than evidence, and Sampson does not show that his taxonomy exhausts relevant realism or that actual moral discourse instantiates every identified component. Live burden: He must progress from the coherent possibility of stance-independent truth to warranted belief in such truth, while preserving his careful existential scope against Bush's semantic and genealogical challenges. Locked score: The move excels in logical coherence, responsiveness, precision, and calibration, but its evidential contribution remains properly modest because fixing the proposition cannot establish that proposition's truth.

moves.sectionTitle: Positions, semantics, and the scope of realism
moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Ordinary moral claims lack a uniform determinate semantics and instead display metaethical indeterminacy and pluralism.

sourceSpan.excerpt: subscribe to any one of the conventional anti-realist positions is because I don't endorse a uniform and determinate account of the meaning of moral claims. So I don't think that all moral claims are, you know, relativized or all of them are implicitly committed to something that's false, it's error theory, or that all of them just express some non-cognitive or non-propositional attitude or something like that. Instead, I endorse a combination

moves.argumentDescription: Bush rejects any uniform semantics for ordinary moral claims, instead proposing an unfinished mixture of relativist, error-theoretic, and noncognitive interpretations across different speakers.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Bush carefully resists forcing every moral utterance into one anti-realist model, and his pluralism fairly recognizes that speakers may express propositions, attitudes, or locally relativized commitments differently. Principal limitation: The excerpt contrasts possible semantic theories without presenting representative linguistic evidence, and its promised positive combination remains insufficiently specified to explain which uses receive which analysis. Live burden: Bush must demonstrate actual variation, formulate principled classification criteria, and explain why pluralism threatens Sampson's existential thesis that merely some communities make shared truth-evaluable claims. Locked score: The move is coherent, responsive, and admirably calibrated, yet limited evidential warrant and incomplete positive detail prevent semantic diversity from establishing either global indeterminacy or the motion-level rejection of realism.

moves.sectionTitle: Positions, semantics, and the scope of realism

moves.proposition: Semantic diversity does not defeat cognitivism because at least some shared moral discourse expresses beliefs evaluable as true or false.

sourceSpan.excerpt: But in any case, there are at least communities of people who mean the same kind of thing and they can speak with one another. responseComponents.text: Semantic variation does not threaten realism because some communities still express shared truth-evaluable moral beliefs.

moves.argumentDescription: Sampson answers pluralism by arguing that realism needs only some communities whose shared moral assertions express beliefs capable of truth or falsity assessment.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson exploits the existential scope of his definition precisely, conceding broad semantic variation while preserving cognitivism wherever communities share moral propositions that they can dispute as true or false. Principal limitation: Plausible communal coordination does not independently prove that the relevant utterances express beliefs, and truth evaluability establishes neither actual truth nor the stance independence required by realism. Live burden: He must support the semantic characterization and then defend non-nihilism and independence, rather than allowing successful resistance to a universal objection to masquerade as positive ontological evidence. Locked score: This is a highly responsive, logically economical, clear, and charitable local rebuttal whose disciplined quantifiers protect one necessary realist component without completing the affirmative's larger evidential burden.

moves.sectionTitle: Whether stance-independent reasons are intelligible
moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Normativity is intelligibly relational to wants or standards, whereas stance-independent reasons do not make sense.

sourceSpan.excerpt: that are best understood as relational. So for instance, if I want to eat food, you could say, you know, if I want to eat food, then I have a reason to eat food. But to me, it doesn't make sense to say that I could have a reason to eat food or I could have a reason to do something independent of what I want or what I desire. Because you're basically

moves.argumentDescription: Bush contends that reasons become intelligible only relative to desires or standards, using hunger to illustrate why desire-independent reasons purportedly make no sense.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The food example gives Bush's relational alternative concrete structure, clearly contrasting reasons generated by an agent's wants with Sampson's proposed reasons that apply regardless of those wants. Principal limitation: One intelligible desire-relative reason does not establish that every intelligible reason must be relational, while Bush's personal incomprehension cannot itself demonstrate contradiction, emptiness, or universal unintelligibility. Live burden: He must define the governing standard of intelligibility, exclude primitive favoring relations without presupposing relationalism, and engage the strongest external-reason account rather than merely reporting unfamiliarity. Locked score: The move directly contacts a central affirmative burden and is relevant if proven, but weak universal warrant, incomplete conceptual analysis, and limited charity substantially constrain its force.

moves.sectionTitle: Whether stance-independent reasons are intelligible
moves.speaker: Eric Sampson
moves.proposition: The child's importance and the benefit of rescue already explain the reason, even if a particular hearer does not understand it.

sourceSpan.excerpt: So, I guess I would say, in this case, the explanation was given, why should I do this? Because that kid matters, and it would cost you almost nothing to jump in and get him, and it would be an enormous benefit for them. That's the explanation. Now, you say, I don't get it. Why should I do that? So, that's asking for a reason. What's the reason? And I'm telling you, the reason is because he matters. Now, you say, that's not, I don't get it. And

responseComponents.text: The child's importance is the explanation; a hearer's failure to grasp it does not show that no explanation was supplied.

moves.argumentDescription: Sampson insists that the child's importance and rescue benefit constitute the requested explanation, treating Bush's continued incomprehension as failure to grasp a primitive reason.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson refuses an infinite regress of explanations and identifies a definite stopping point, treating the child's welfare and inexpensive rescue as publicly stated facts that normatively explain intervention. Principal limitation: Repeating that the child matters may clarify the proposed reason without vindicating its irreducible authority, and the move too quickly converts Bush's dissatisfaction into defective understanding. Live burden: Sampson must justify primitive normative explanation, distinguish it from mere assertion, and offer some basis for preferring his stopping point over Bush's desire-relative reconstruction of the same conduct. Locked score: The response is direct, coherent, and unusually clear about its explanatory commitment, yet intuitive warrant and limited engagement with the rival analysis leave stance-independent truth unestablished.

finalDimensionRationales.logicalCoherence: The response consistently identifies welfare facts as reasons, but repeating them does not fully answer a request for their normative connection.
finalDimensionRationales.evidenceWarrant: The welfare and cost facts support rescue, but warrant for treating 'he matters' as irreducibly explanatory is largely intuitive.
finalDimensionRationales.responsiveness: It answers the demand by naming the proposed explanation, yet leaves the opponent's concern about how those facts generate reasons unresolved.
finalDimensionRationales.relevanceBurden: The reply keeps the central affirmative explanation in view, but its success depends on accepting the very normative understanding under dispute.
finalDimensionRationales.precisionClarity: The claimed reason and explanatory facts are stated plainly, with the hearer's failure to grasp them clearly distinguished.
finalDimensionRationales.calibrationCharity: The response fairly recognizes continued incomprehension, though it somewhat understates the opponent's request for a deeper conceptual account.

moves.sectionTitle: Whether stance-independent reasons are intelligible
moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Claimed private understanding of external reasons is inadequate without a publicly communicable explanation of their meaning.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Yeah, so people can say they make sense of it, but okay, then can they explain it? So, like, one of my concerns about this is that to the extent that people say they can make sense of it, it seems like it's like they could privately make sense of it, but they can't explain how it makes sense. And this isn't typical of most things. So, you know, if someone says,

responseComponents.text: Merely reporting private understanding does not publicly explain what an attitude-independent reason is.

moves.argumentDescription: Bush argues that privately claiming to understand stance-independent reasons is inadequate unless one can publicly explain what those reasons mean and how they make sense.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Bush identifies an important dialectical difference between experiencing comprehension and communicating an explanation capable of showing another participant what a disputed concept means and how it operates. Principal limitation: He leaves the required explanatory standard unspecified and risks assuming that genuine understanding always permits reductive elaboration, thereby excluding primitive concepts through a criterion the argument never defends. Live burden: Bush must explain what public account would suffice, demonstrate that stance-independent favoring fails that standard, and establish that comparable foundational concepts do not face the same stopping point. Locked score: The reply sharply advances the intelligibility dispute and directly tests Sampson's example, but limited evidence and an underdefined criterion prevent reported explanatory dissatisfaction from proving conceptual incoherence.

Because remember, we're telling you these are non-natural moral facts. They're not identical to any particular empirical entity that's out there. moves.critique: Strongest feature: Sampson correctly notes that evidence must fit the proposed ontology, making absence of a physical moral-property detector expected under non-naturalism rather than a surprising failure that straightforwardly disconfirms it. moves.sectionTitle: Corroboration, intuition, and prima facie justification
moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Unlike engineering or medicine, moral realism offers no independent test for corroborating competing accounts of what ought to be done.

sourceSpan.excerpt: and the same would hold for engineering or biology or medicine. If someone's understanding of how to conduct, how to perform a surgery or how to fix a car or how to build a bridge is wrong, the bridge is going to collapse. The person's going to die on the operating table. I don't see any comparable standard of independent corroboration to find out if a particular account of why we should morally do or not do something is true. It's just people

moves.argumentDescription: Bush contrasts morality with engineering, biology, and medicine, arguing that realism lacks comparable independent consequences capable of corroborating theories and adjudicating disagreements.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The cross-disciplinary comparison crystallizes a serious epistemic asymmetry, asking what publicly accessible consequence could discriminate rival moral accounts when first-order intuitions and judgments remain fundamentally contested. Principal limitation: Empirical disciplines may set an inappropriate standard for non-natural facts, and Bush does not establish that every justified domain requires detection, prediction, or practical confirmation of the illustrated kind. Live burden: He must specify a suitably general corroboration requirement, defend its applicability to normativity, and explain whether coherent reflection or explanatory success could satisfy it without becoming circular. Locked score: The move strongly advances the public-adjudication burden through clear and relevant comparisons, but incomplete defense of their comparability prevents absent empirical testing from independently defeating realism.

moves.sectionTitle: Deep disagreement and the Zorpian comparison
moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: A culturally shaped alien normative system could reproduce realist argumentative moves, creating parity with claims humans regard as false.

moves.argumentDescription: Bush imagines competitively evolved Zorpians with contrary but structurally similar normative intuitions, challenging whether Sampson's method can distinguish truth from cultural conditioning.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The detailed alien society converts abstract reliability worries into a discriminating parity test, showing how contrary attitudes, intuitions, and realist arguments might arise from an alternative selective history. Principal limitation: The analogy depends on matching every epistemically relevant feature, and its deliberately abhorrent competitive norms may encourage intuitive rejection without establishing that Zorpian evidence genuinely equals human evidence. Live burden: Bush must specify the parity conditions, explain why evolutionary origin defeats rather than merely causes belief, and show that no independent substantive reason breaks the symmetry. Locked score: The thought experiment strongly pressures intuitive realism with considerable relevance, clarity, and methodological ingenuity, but its reliability conclusion remains conditional upon an incompletely defended comparison.

moves.argumentDescription: Bush argues that widespread professions of understanding cannot establish intelligibility, comparing them with consensus about contradictory or invented concepts that remain meaningless.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Bush correctly denies entailment from widespread claimed comprehension to genuine intelligibility, and his counterexamples reveal that testimony alone cannot guarantee that a purported concept possesses coherent content. Principal limitation: Comparing stance-independent reasons with square circles or deliberate nonsense assumes the relevant defect without demonstrating contradiction, inferential emptiness, or comparable semantic failure in normative discourse. Live burden: Bush must provide a positive criterion of meaningfulness and show how realist reasons violate it, rather than relying on skeptical possibilities that could undermine many theoretically primitive concepts. Locked score: The move directly limits consensus-based proof with clear reasoning, but weak analogy, underspecified standards, and incomplete charity leave the original intelligibility objection protected rather than affirmatively established.

overallBlunders.speaker: Eric Sampson
overallBlunders.text: Sampson repeatedly moves too quickly from objective-seeming intuitions to objective facts, without supplying a reliability account capable of defeating projection or incompatible Zorpian intuitions.

overallBlunders.speaker: Eric Sampson
overallBlunders.text: His answer to Zorpian parity largely relabels attitude-independent alien reasons as moral facts, leaving the actual problem of discriminating contradictory substantive judgments unresolved.

overallBlunders.speaker: Eric Sampson
overallBlunders.text: His parsimony reply risks assuming realism by counting normative facts among established explananda, rather than independently identifying phenomena that psychological anti-realism cannot explain.

overallBlunders.speaker: Lance Bush
overallBlunders.text: Bush's foundational relationalism leans heavily on personal unintelligibility and a desire-relative example, neither of which establishes the universal claim that all intelligible reasons are conditional.

overallBlunders.speaker: Lance Bush
overallBlunders.text: His comparison with empirical disciplines demands independent corroboration without adequately defending why non-natural normative claims must satisfy engineering-style prediction or detection standards.

overallBlunders.speaker: Lance Bush
overallBlunders.text: His academic selection and cultural-biological explanations remain largely prospective, lacking data, operational criteria, or a demonstrated link from causal contingency to epistemic unreliability or falsity.

definitions.label: Appeal to authority
definitions.definition: Relying on a person or institution's status as if it settles the argument, especially when the relevant evidence, expertise, or consensus has not been shown.

definitions.label: Argument from ignorance
definitions.definition: Treating a claim as true because it has not been disproved, or false because it has not been proved, rather than supplying positive evidence.

definitions.label: Begging the question
definitions.definition: Assuming, directly or indirectly, the very point that needs to be established, so the conclusion is smuggled into the premises.

definitions.label: Equivocation
definitions.definition: Shifting the meaning of a key word or phrase during the argument, making the reasoning seem stronger than it is.

definitions.label: Red herring
definitions.definition: Diverting attention from the issue under dispute to a related but less relevant point, leaving the original challenge insufficiently answered.

definitions.label: Special pleading
definitions.definition: Applying an exception or different standard to one side of the argument without giving a principled reason for the difference.

definitions.label: Ambiguity effect
definitions.definition: Preferring clearer or more familiar claims over uncertain ones, even when the uncertain option may deserve serious consideration.

definitions.label: Authority bias
definitions.definition: Giving extra weight to a claim because it comes from a perceived authority, sometimes beyond what the evidence itself supports.

definitions.label: Base-rate neglect
definitions.definition: Underweighting general background rates or prior probabilities while focusing too heavily on a vivid specific case or local detail.

definitions.label: Belief bias
definitions.definition: Judging an argument by whether its conclusion feels believable instead of evaluating whether the conclusion follows from the premises.

definitions.label: Confirmation bias
definitions.definition: Seeking, interpreting, or remembering evidence in ways that favor an existing view while discounting contrary information.

definitions.label: Scope neglect
definitions.definition: Failing to adjust judgment in proportion to the scale, number, or magnitude of what is being discussed.

definitions.label: Subjective validation
definitions.definition: Treating a claim as especially accurate or meaningful because it feels personally resonant or confirms one's private experience.
